card.hook: Picture a pyramid of hand-stacked clay bricks, with modern apartment blocks peeking over its shoulder. That's Huaca Pucllana, and it sits right in the middle of Miraflores.
card.stand_here: Head to Huaca Pucllana on General Borgoño (block 8) in Miraflores. The phone icon on the map is at the site itself, so there's no extra walk. Face the stepped pyramid.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole pyramid in one shot. Switch to 0.5x near the entrance to squeeze in the yellow façade, the adobe wall and the street. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the brick rows and their shadows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the stepped edges with them, then tap the brightest part of the pyramid and drag the slider a little darker so the lit bricks don't wash out.
card.best_time: Arrive around sunset and stay into the evening, when the pyramid is lit up and the light and shadow play across the bricks. Go before the lights go off, which is about 10:30 pm, though that may change. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone against a wall or rail until it finishes.
card.selfie_here: Try the reflection pool just inside the entrance: use the front camera, hold the phone low, and let the pyramid's reflection fill the water behind you. For a spikier backdrop, the cactus garden puts cacti up front and adobe walls behind you. Both are worth a quick check when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the visitor routes, don't lean on the walls for a photo, and never climb on the ruins. Some museum rooms have no-photo signs, and selfie sticks are often not allowed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a shot where the ancient bricks and a modern apartment block share the frame, and see whether you can make them look like neighbours.
card.good_to_know: The pyramid is built from seven staggered platforms of adobe and clay. It was a ceremonial and administrative centre of the Lima Culture, who lived on Peru's central coast between about 200 and 700 AD. The enclosure is over 500 metres long, 100 metres wide and 22 metres high, and the site museum opened in 1984.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Huaca Pucllana on General Borgoño (block 8) in Miraflores. The phone icon on the map is at the site itself, so there's no extra walk. Face the stepped pyramid.

card.hook: Here's a museum where the building steals the show before you've even bought a ticket. It's an 18th-century vice-royal house in Lima's Pueblo Libre, and it's a photo before you walk through the door.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map. It sits at the Larco Museum itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the building and step back as far as visitors are allowed so its lines fit in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and the display cases. Switch to 0.5x in tight courtyards or to squeeze in more of the front. Go to 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for details on ceramics and gold pieces.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Outside, daylight gives you the cleanest views of the building. Inside, the lighting is fixed, so go earlier or at a quieter moment to get clear access to the cases.
card.selfie_here: Try the walkway from the entrance to the exhibition rooms, where flowers and vines climb the walls. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the blooms fill the space behind your shoulder. For a dusk selfie, the Cafe Museo Larco courtyard by the colonial arches is lit softly in the evening.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in Parque Larco, opposite the museum entrance on Calle Navarra 169, to take your photo with the white mansion in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed in the exhibition rooms or the gardens. Flash isn't permitted in the exhibition rooms, and neither are amateur or professional photo sessions. Rules can differ from room to room, so watch for signs and ask staff if you're unsure.
card.challenge: Find one gold ornament or ceramic piece and fill the whole frame with it, with zero you in the glass reflection.
card.good_to_know: The collection began in 1925, when Rafael Larco Herrera acquired around 600 ceramic pieces. His son, Rafael Larco Hoyle, built it up, and the museum first opened to the public on 28 July 1926, Peru's Independence Day. The galleries take you through about 5,000 years of Peruvian history, and there's a Gold and Silver Gallery with crowns, earrings and masks.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map. It sits at the Larco Museum itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Face the building and step back as far as visitors are allowed so its lines fit in.

card.hook: Picture a shopping centre that skipped the back wall and just let the Pacific in. That's Larcomar: terraces stepping down a cliff edge, with the whole coastline opening up in front of you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open-air terrace at Larcomar that faces San Lorenzo Island. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk once you're inside. Face the island and the sea.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main terrace view, then tap 0.5x to squeeze in more cliff and coastline. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out San Lorenzo Island or details along the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or sea, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Aim for about an hour before sunset. You'll grab a spot at the railing before the terrace fills up. After the sun has gone, try night mode and rest your phone on the railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the terrace railing that faces San Lorenzo Island and turn your back to the ocean, with the sea and sunset behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it to fit more sky in. Heads up: Larcomar itself won't be in this shot, it's all sea behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The mall has its own opening hours, and some terraces may be for restaurant customers only at times, so check the official site before you go. The open-air terraces are free to walk into, though a drink or meal is often expected if you want a seat.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, and see if you can keep it perfectly level. Over open water it's very obvious when it isn't!
card.good_to_know: Larcomar opened on 27 November 1998 and was designed by architect Eduardo Figari Gold. You walk in through Alfredo Salazar Park, which has a scenic overlook, a children's playground and a statue of Paddington Bear added in 2015. If the terrace is packed, Parque del Amor along the coast is a separate sunset spot with the El Beso sculpture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open-air terrace at Larcomar that faces San Lorenzo Island. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk once you're inside. Face the island and the sea.

card.hook: Parque Kennedy gives you two pictures from one patch of Lima: a busy scene on the amphitheatre steps, and a calm one with pale church towers peeking through leaves and flowers. Pick your mood.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, inside the park at the amphitheatre's curved seating. Face the people on the steps, and for the quiet shot, turn and walk a little way off so you're facing the church towers.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for people on the steps, or zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole curve of the seating. Switch to zoom 2x to bring the church towers closer over the flower beds.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and let the curved steps run diagonally from a bottom corner towards the people, so the lines pull the eye into the scene.
card.best_time: Evenings are your best bet, when couples gather and concerts or dancing are more likely. If it's getting dark, let night mode do its thing and hold your phone steady against your body.
card.selfie_here: One Lima guide calls the bull statue inside the park a popular selfie place, though it doesn't say exactly where in the park it is, so keep an eye out for it as you wander. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and see what you can get over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from a spot in the park facing the Virgen Milagrosa church, while you stand in front of it, so you're framed against the church towers and trees.
card.rules_and_safety: Be polite when people are in your shot, and ask first if you want a close portrait.
card.challenge: Get one photo where the curve of the steps runs diagonally through the frame and a stranger's perfectly timed moment (a laugh, a dance step) lands right in the middle.
card.good_to_know: Parque Kennedy is a city park with flower beds, shade trees and an amphitheatre with curved seating. Small concerts and dancing often happen here, so it feels most alive when people gather. Cats and street performers wander through too, but nothing is guaranteed on any one day.

card.hook: Two matching bell towers, a fountain in front and a palace on each side: the Plaza Mayor has basically set this shot up for you. All you have to do is stand in the right place and keep your phone straight.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Plaza Mayor, facing the cathedral front with the central fountain in front of you. From the plaza, the cathedral is to the south-east, about 2 minutes on foot across the plaza.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade, the fountain and the palaces into one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the towers and the carved doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand straight, then tap the facade and nudge it darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, when the light is softer and the square is quieter. If people are crossing, wait a moment for a gap, or let them show how big the building is.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the open square in front of the cathedral facade, which is the classic view, so use the front camera at 0.5x with the cathedral over your shoulder. For a different look, try Calle de la Inquisición beside the cathedral, where colonial buildings frame the facade, best in golden hour (it's from a single guide, so check it on the map first).
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the open square in front of the facade, far enough back to fit the whole building, and to crouch a little, because a low angle shows off its height.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the cathedral, flash is generally not allowed, and photography can be restricted in places like chapels or during services, so check the signs. Photos for personal use are allowed.
card.challenge: Can you get both towers perfectly straight, the fountain at the bottom and not a single stranger's head in the frame? Give it three tries.
card.good_to_know: This spot was once an Inca shrine and the home of an Inca prince, and Francisco Pizarro laid the first stone in 1535. Earthquakes, including a bad one in 1746, meant repeated rebuilding, and the building took its present form between 1602 and 1797. The current bell towers date from 1794 to 1797.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: the phone icon drops you at the centre of the convent, not out front where the famous yellow facade is. Walk to the front of the church before you start snapping.
card.stand_here: For the facade, stand in Plaza San Francisco in front of the entrance, if it's open, and face the church so both towers are in view. The square has been reported closed to the public since August 2022, so check the situation before you plan around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade and both towers. If you can't get far enough back, try 0.5x, but hold the phone level so the towers don't lean inwards. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the tower tops and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up the middle of the facade with the centre of the frame, and keep a strip of the square at the bottom for scale.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun isn't directly behind the facade, because it can turn the front dark. Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Head for Plazuela San Francisco, at the corner of Jirón Áncash and Jirón Lampa, and stand on the square with the yellow facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the towers, and tilt the phone up a little so the church sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and videos aren't allowed inside the convent and the catacombs, and flash isn't allowed. The catacomb tunnels have narrow passages and stairs, which may not suit anyone with severe claustrophobia or reduced mobility.
card.challenge: Get both towers perfectly balanced on the gridlines, with a slice of the square at the bottom, and see if you can do it without a stranger wandering into the shot.
card.good_to_know: Lima was founded in 1535, and the Franciscans got land in the new city soon after. An earthquake in February 1655 brought the first convent down, and the rebuilt one was inaugurated in October 1672. The church became a minor basilica in 1963, and the Historic Centre of Lima joined UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1991.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: For the facade, stand in Plaza San Francisco in front of the entrance, if it's open, and face the church so both towers are in view. The square has been reported closed to the public since August 2022, so check the situation before you plan around it.

card.hook: This palace is wider than your phone wants it to be, and that's the fun of it. The Lima Art Museum (MALI) has a long, symmetrical, classical frontage that looks great once you back up far enough.
card.stand_here: Start in front of the Palacio de la Exposición in Exposition Park, right where the phone icon on the map sits. Then step back as far as the space allows and face the façade so the whole width fits.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if you're close, since the building is so wide. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details higher up on the façade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the centre of the building up with the middle of the frame, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest, because the façade is evenly lit. Early or late can give softer light, but check where the sun falls on the building first.
card.selfie_here: Head to the central ornamental fountain in front of the palace, which a park guide calls the best-known in the park and a popular photo spot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the palace over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside MALI, photos and video are allowed for personal use without flash, and selfie sticks aren't permitted. Check the official site before you go for current access to the museum and the park.
card.challenge: Get the building perfectly symmetrical on the gridlines, then take a second shot with only a small section of the façade filling the frame.
card.good_to_know: The palace was built for the 1872 World's Fair. Its Italianate façade, designed by Antonio Leonardi, wraps around an iron structure that came from Gustave Eiffel's workshop in 1870-71. The museum opened in 1961 and covers almost 3,000 years of Peruvian art.

card.hook: Picture a pedestrian street full of shoppers, all leading your eye to a square where the buildings look like they agreed on a dress code. That's Plaza San Martín, and it makes a tidy backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jirón de la Unión, at the end of the pedestrian street nearest Plaza San Martín. Face the plaza's grand buildings, so the street's facades and passing shoppers lead your eye in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x on the street, which keeps the buildings looking natural. Once you're in the square, switch to 0.5x to fit the statue and the facades into one frame. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the statue or the arcade columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines, so the tall buildings don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Go in the morning if you can. The light reaches down the street before the coastal mist (garúa) settles in. Wait a moment for a gap in the crowd.
card.selfie_here: Head to the middle of the square and stand next to the big San Martín statue with the monument behind you. Reviewers pick it as the go-to selfie backdrop. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit more of the monument in.
card.ask_someone: Stand by the monument and ask a passer-by to step back across the paved square, away from the statue base, so their photo takes in you, the monument and the buildings around it.
card.rules_and_safety: The city centre is crowded, so stay alert for pickpockets and keep your belongings secure.
card.challenge: Get a shot down Jirón de la Unión with a shopper walking through the foreground, and keep the building edges straight on your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: The plaza opened on 27 July 1921 to mark 100 years of Peruvian independence. Manuel Piqueras Cotolí designed the layout, and the monument to José de San Martín is by the sculptor Mariano Benlliure. The buildings around it went up in stages between 1914 and 1945 but share a similar neocolonial look, including the Hotel Bolívar (1924) and the Zela and Pumacahua arcades (1926).
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jirón de la Unión, at the end of the pedestrian street nearest Plaza San Martín. Face the plaza's grand buildings, so the street's facades and passing shoppers lead your eye in.

card.best_time: Go in the late afternoon, when the light is warm and the changing of the guard usually happens. Times can vary, so check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the central bronze fountain (Fountain of Pizarro) in the middle of the square, with the colonial facades behind you. card.rules_and_safety: Photography in the square is allowed, but ask permission before photographing individuals. Flash is often banned inside the Cathedral, and some areas may be restricted, so check signs or ask staff. Be careful with street vendors, as scams and pickpocketing are possible.

card.good_to_know: Francisco Pizarro founded Lima here on 18 January 1535. In 1821 José de San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence in this square. The fountain in the middle was inaugurated on 8 September 1651 and is still the centrepiece.

card.hook: Picture a long, fancy palace front, a bronze fountain right in front of it, and a row of guards in bright red uniforms. That's Lima's Plaza Mayor at its most photogenic, and the noon crowd knows it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the bronze fountain in the middle of Plaza Mayor and face the Government Palace, which fills the north side of the square. Stop once the whole facade fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the palace and the colonial buildings in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the facade. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the guards and the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain in the lower part of the frame, keep the phone level so the long lines stay straight, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when warm light hits the yellow colonial buildings around the plaza. For fewer people in your shot, come early, before the tour groups. If you want the Changing of the Guard, arrive before noon to get a clear view.
card.selfie_here: Pose beside the octagonal bronze fountain in the middle of the square, with the colonial facades behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt it until a good slice of the buildings sits over your shoulder, then check the framing on the spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the edge of the square on the north side, facing the palace front, so the whole facade and the square fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The palace interior isn't open to independent visitors, so all your pictures are taken from the square outside. Visit in daylight, because the streets around the Plaza de Armas can be dangerous at night.
card.challenge: Catch one guard in red uniform framed against the palace facade, and keep the horizon dead level while you do it.
card.good_to_know: The Government Palace is where Peru's president works and lives. Francisco Pizarro built the first palace here in 1535, and fires in 1884 and 1921 destroyed much of the later building. What you see today went up between 1926 and 1938, with a Neo-Baroque-inspired facade designed by Ricardo de Jaxa Malachowski.

card.hook: Picture a tall jet of water shooting up in front of a row of tidy neoclassical arches. That's the Fuente Mágica, and it hands you a ready-made park panorama before you've even tried.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Fuente Mágica and face the Logia colonnade, so the tall central jet sits in front of the arches. Small steps left or right change how the arches line up behind the water, so shuffle a bit before you settle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the jet with the arches behind it. If the whole colonnade won't fit, switch to zoom 0.5x. For the Pumawasi cascade, try zoom 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the jet on a vertical line so the arches sit evenly on both sides, and keep the horizon level because any tilt shows up against the colonnade.
card.best_time: The Fantasy Fountain show runs in the evening, and the Pumawasi cascade looks calmer in daylight. Show times change with the season and the day, so check the schedule and arrive early if you want a front spot.
card.selfie_here: Head for the Tunnel of Surprises (Fuente Túnel de las Sorpresas) and pose inside the 35-metre walk-through water arch. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so the arch curves over your shoulder, and keep to the right side of the tunnel to stay dry.
card.rules_and_safety: The park needs an entrance ticket, so check the official site for prices and show times. One guide says photos are fine for non-commercial use, but a review mentions photo fees, so check the rules when you arrive. Keep your phone put away until you're through the gates.
card.challenge: Get the jet dead centre on a gridline with the arches perfectly level, then try the same shot with a friend pretending to hold the water up.
card.good_to_know: The Circuito Mágico del Agua is a park of illuminated fountains inside Parque de la Reserva in Lima. The Fantasy Fountain throws up a water screen about 120 metres wide, and in the evening show, jets and laser light form images on it. The Catarata de Pumawasi is a cascade of roughly 12 metres, lit by daylight.

card.hook: Red and gold, perfectly symmetrical, and standing right at the mouth of Lima's Chinatown: the Chinese Arch is hard to miss, and it practically asks to be photographed.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Jirón Ucayali and Jirón Andahuaylas, straight in front of the Calle Capón face of the arch. Face the arch so it's centred, with a guardian lion on each side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on, symmetrical shot. If the crowds push you in close, switch to 0.5x to fit the whole gateway in, then try 2x for the lions and the Chinese characters on the top beam.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the middle of the arch on the centre line so both lions balance, and keep your phone level so the gateway doesn't look lopsided.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can. The crowds are thinner, so a clear frontal shot is much easier.
card.selfie_here: Try Calle Capón, in front of the arch next to the Central Market, which one Lima travel blog calls a must-take shot. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the arch in behind your shoulder so it fills the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand straight in front of the arch for the symmetrical frame, while you stand in front of the gate, centred between the lions.
card.rules_and_safety: There's no charge to photograph the arch, but the street can be busy and uneven, so watch your step while you line up your shot. One guide suggests registered ride-hailing apps such as Uber for getting around.
card.challenge: Zoom in to 2x and catch the characters on the top beam, which on the Calle Capón side read 'Under the same sky, we are all equal'.
card.good_to_know: The Chinese Arch (Arco Chino) is a paifang, a traditional Chinese-style gateway. It was a gift from Lima's Chinese community and the government of Taiwan, marking 150 years of Peruvian independence, and was inaugurated on 12 November 1971. It stands 8 metres high and 13 metres wide, and the two guardian lions were unveiled in 2017.

card.hook: From the street, Casa de Aliaga looks fairly plain, and then you look up. The dark carved wooden balconies are the real show, and most people walk right under them.
card.stand_here: Start in Plaza Mayor de Lima and face the fountain, palms and cathedral façade for your scene-setter. From the plaza, Casa de Aliaga is to the north, about 3 minutes on foot. Stand close to the wall there and face up at the balconies.

card.make_it_pop: Tap the balconies, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) if the sky is bright, so the dark wood keeps its detail.

card.selfie_here: The courtyard fountain inside Casa de Aliaga is the house's main photo area. Stand beside the fountain with the wooden balconies and galleries behind you, use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of them in.

card.challenge: Find the balcony with the darkest carving and get it sitting against the lighter wall, with no one's head in the shot (good luck).
card.good_to_know: The house dates back to May 1536, the first years of Lima's founding, and was built for the conquistador Geronimo de Aliaga. It stands on a huaca, a pre-Hispanic sacred site. The same family is said to have lived here for seventeen generations over five centuries. The 1746 earthquake destroyed it, and it was rebuilt, with more work in the 19th century, which explains the mix of styles.

card.hook: From the street, Acho is mostly a big wall. From up the hill, it turns into a neat red circle with a river and a whole city behind it. That's the picture you came for.
card.stand_here: Stand at the summit lookout on Cerro San Cristóbal and face the bullring below you. Check the route up before you go, because the hill and the bullring are two different places.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the ring, the Rímac river and the city beyond in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the ring closer and fill the frame with its circle.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the bullring and slide to darker if the bright sky is washing out the colours.
card.best_time: Pick a clear part of the day when the city isn't hazy, so the ring and the centre of Lima behind it stay sharp.
card.selfie_here: Try the grand central arch of the Paseo de Aguas on Jirón Madera, near the bullring, which one page calls a popular photo spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the arch behind you. It's a nearby backdrop, not a confirmed bullring selfie.
card.rules_and_safety: Check access to the hill lookout before you go. The arena may be closed outside the Sunday bullfight season in October and November, so check the official site. One visitor found the Paseo de Aguas a little unsafe, so keep your phone out of sight there.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot from the hill and one close-up of the ring, then see which one makes you say "wow" first.
card.good_to_know: Acho opened on 30 January 1766, making it the oldest bullring in the Americas and the second-oldest in the world, after La Maestranza in Spain. It holds 13,700 people and was built of adobe and wood. The land was once called "el Hacho", a Quechua word for an elevated place with a view, which suits the hilltop photo.

card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then tap the church front and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the white and pink tower doesn't wash out against the sky.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, or whenever the light hits the front from the side, because it brings out the carving and the texture of the walls. If you're heading into the cloister, a guide suggests midday, when sunlight streams through the arches.
card.selfie_here: Head into the first courtyard of the convent (Jirón Camaná 170 entrance) and stand with the bell tower behind you. Use the front camera, try the 0.5x button if your phone has it, and let the mosaic-lined walls add colour.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo from Jirón Camaná at the church front, one block west of the Plaza de Armas, so the facade and tower both fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash inside the church or on artworks, and rules about photos inside can vary, so check posted signs. The tower stair is steep and narrow, and the tower needs a ticket and a guided visit, so check current ticket details and opening hours before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom to 5x, find the trumpet-blowing angel, and get her sitting right on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: The bell tower was designed in 1766 in the Rococo style, and the base still shows the rough, blocky stonework from the first church's front. Earthquakes destroyed that first church in 1678, so what you see today is layered from several rebuilds. The church became a Minor Basilica in 1930 and holds the relics of Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plazuela de Santo Domingo, with the church to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. Face the church front so the bell tower and a balcony or two fit in the frame.

card.hook: You'll spot this one from across the square, because it's the big, cheerful yellow wall with wooden balconies and no interest in blending in. It's one of the easiest buildings on Plaza Mayor to photograph, so it's a good place to warm up.
card.stand_here: Head to Plaza Mayor in Lima's Historic Centre, then look for the Palacio Municipal about 95 m to the north-west, roughly 2 minutes on foot. Stand out in the open plaza (the central fountain works well) and face north-west so the yellow facade fills your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from the plaza to fit the whole front in. Use 2x or more, if your phone has it, to pick out the balconies and arcade. In the narrow side passage, zoom 0.5x helps you squeeze the wall and balconies in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the arcade up with a horizontal line so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early or late in the day usually gives softer light. Honestly, though, the facade looks good at most times of day.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the western side of Plaza Mayor with the Palacio's yellow front and wooden balconies behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x so more of the building fits, and keep the yellow wall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the central fountain while you stand on the western side of the square with the Palacio behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Plazas in the historic centre are freely photographable, but the palace is a government building and the area around it can close at times. Check for closures before you set up.
card.challenge: Catch someone strolling across the square so the yellow wall and balconies look busy and alive behind them.
card.good_to_know: The town council has been on this site since 1548, when it moved to land that had belonged to Hernando Pizarro. The 1746 Lima-Callao earthquake destroyed about 90% of the city's colonial civil buildings. So what you see today came after the early council houses, which were fairly plain.

card.hook: Look up: the whole front of La Merced is carved stone, and the Virgin of Mercy sits right in the middle of it in her own little niche. The street around it is busy, but the front is the reason you stopped.
card.stand_here: Stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Jirón de la Unión, and face south-east towards the church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because the street is narrow and the church is tall. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the front, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved entrance and the statue in its niche.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the tower and entrance with the vertical lines, keeping your phone level so the building doesn't lean backwards.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the street is quieter and it's easiest to get a clear view of the front.
card.selfie_here: Head for the small Plazuela de la Merced on Jirón de la Unión, right in front of the church. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if yours has it) and put the carved façade behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plazuela across from the front of the church, on Jirón de la Unión, so the full façade and tower fit in the frame, while you pose with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside and inside are fine, but flash isn't allowed, and photography may be restricted during services, so follow staff instructions. Vendors near the plaza may hand out holy cards and then ask for payment, so you can politely say no. If you want to go inside, check the official site first for visiting rules.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide to show the church in its street, then one close-up where the Virgin of Mercy fills the frame in her niche.
card.good_to_know: La Merced is as old as the city itself. The stone entrance dates from 1696, and the tower, staircase and interior balconies were rebuilt between 1759 and 1762 after earthquake damage. Early in the 20th century the front was covered in thick plaster in a French-looking style, and that was removed in 1940, so you're now seeing the original face of the building.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 35 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map near Jirón de la Unión, and face south-east towards the church.

card.hook: Picture a pale, detailed front with ornate cedar balconies hanging over the doors, and a stone saint watching from the roof. That's the Archbishop's Palace, and it's a lot more photogenic than you'd expect.
card.stand_here: Stand out in the open Plaza Mayor (also called Plaza de Armas), facing the palace on the east side of the square, right next to the cathedral. Step back until the whole front fits on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade with the cathedral beside it. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the front, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved balconies and the statue on the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the facade, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is glaring, so the pale stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Afternoon is likely to be kinder, because the front faces across the square to the west. Early in the day it may sit more in shade.
card.selfie_here: Stand out in the Plaza Mayor with your back to the palace, so the carved wooden balconies sit behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and try 0.5x if it's on your phone. If you go inside, the grand staircase is another popular selfie backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out in the Plaza Mayor facing the palace so the whole facade fits, while you stand in front of the building with the balconies behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Some areas inside the palace may restrict photography, especially near religious artifacts, so check before taking pictures indoors. The outside is fine to photograph from the open square.
card.challenge: Find the granite statue on the roofline and get it in one shot with a flag fluttering beside it.
card.good_to_know: Francisco Pizarro set this land aside for Lima's head priest after the city was founded in 1535. The building you see today is much newer: it opened on 8 December 1924 in Spanish Colonial Revival style. Its architect, Ricardo de Jaxa Malachowski, took the Torre Tagle Palace as a reference. The statue on top is Saint Turibius of Mongrovejo, patron protector of the Archdiocese.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand out in the open Plaza Mayor (also called Plaza de Armas), facing the palace on the east side of the square, right next to the cathedral. Step back until the whole front fits on your screen.
